opening_arguments.for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

I stand for the proposition that **Islam promotes peace**. This does not mean that every Muslim has always acted peacefully, nor that Islam is a pacifist tradition with no concept of self-defense. Rather, it means that the core teachings of Islam—its scripture, ethics, law, and vision of human society—aim to establish peace with God, peace within the self, and peace among people.

The very greeting Muslims are encouraged to spread is **“as-salamu ‘alaykum” — “peace be upon you.”** Peace is not a slogan in Islam; it is a daily moral practice.

First, Islam promotes peace by affirming the sanctity of human life. The Qur’an declares:

> “Whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had slain all mankind; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all mankind.”  
> **Qur’an 5:32**

This is one of the strongest possible statements against murder and indiscriminate violence. Human life is sacred, and saving life is treated as a service to all humanity.

Second, Islam promotes peace by rejecting forced religion. The Qur’an states plainly:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> **Qur’an 2:256**

A faith that forbids coercion in belief cannot honestly be described as inherently violent or oppressive. Islam calls people to persuasion, conscience, and moral example—not forced conversion.

Third, Islam promotes peaceful coexistence and justice even with those who are different. The Qur’an says:

> “O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another.”  
> **Qur’an 49:13**

Difference is presented not as a reason for hatred, but as an opportunity for mutual knowledge. The Qur’an also says:

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion or driven you from your homes.”  
> **Qur’an 60:8**

So kindness and justice toward non-Muslims are not exceptions; they are Qur’anic principles.

Fourth, Islam commands justice even toward enemies. The Qur’an warns:

> “Do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”  
> **Qur’an 5:8**

This is a profound peace ethic. Many ideologies preach loyalty to one’s own group; Islam demands justice even when emotions, politics, or tribal loyalties push in the opposite direction.

Fifth, while Islam does permit fighting in self-defense, it places moral limits on conflict. The Qur’an says:

> “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love transgressors.”  
> **Qur’an 2:190**

And another passage explains that permission to fight was given to those who had been wronged and driven from their homes, adding that without such defense, monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques would be destroyed.  
**Qur’an 22:39–40**

This shows that the purpose of legitimate defense is not aggression, domination, or forced conversion, but protection from persecution and preservation of religious freedom.

Sixth, the Prophet Muhammad’s teachings reinforce this peaceful moral vision. He said:

> “The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 10; Sahih Muslim 40**

In another narration, he taught:

> “The merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on the earth…”  
> **Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 1924**

These teachings define religious character not by violence, cruelty, or domination, but by safety, mercy, and restraint.

Finally, Islam promotes peace because it teaches that reconciliation is better than hostility. The Qur’an says:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”  
> **Qur’an 8:61**

And:

> “Repel evil with what is better.”  
> **Qur’an 41:34**

That is not the language of a religion seeking endless conflict. It is the language of moral discipline, forgiveness, and peacemaking.

So the proposition before us is not that Muslims have always lived up to Islam’s ideals. No religious or political community can make that claim. The question is whether Islam itself promotes peace. Its scripture honors life, forbids religious compulsion, commands justice, encourages reconciliation, restricts warfare to defense, and teaches mercy as a mark of true faith.

For these reasons, I strongly affirm: **Islam promotes peace.**
opening_arguments.against:
Ladies and gentlemen, I oppose the motion “Islam promotes peace” not because Muslims cannot be peaceful—millions are—but because the proposition is too broad. A religion should be judged not only by the virtues of many of its followers, but also by its foundational texts, legal tradition, and historical political theology. On that basis, Islam does not consistently promote peace as a universal principle; it promotes peace conditionally—often after submission to Islamic authority.

The Qur’an certainly contains passages encouraging restraint and reconciliation, but it also contains explicit commands to fight. For example, Qur’an 9:29 instructs Muslims to “fight those who do not believe” among the People of the Book “until they pay the jizya with willing submission.” Qur’an 9:5 commands fighting against polytheists after the sacred months unless they repent and accept Islam. Qur’an 8:39 says to fight “until there is no fitna and religion is entirely for Allah.” These are not merely abstract spiritual metaphors; they became part of a legal and political tradition of jihad.

The Hadith literature reinforces this. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Muhammad is reported as saying: “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…” (Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22). Another hadith says: “Whoever changes his religion, kill him” (Sahih al-Bukhari 3017), a text that became a basis for classical apostasy laws. These are difficult to reconcile with the claim that Islam, as a system, simply “promotes peace.”

Classical Islamic jurisprudence also developed doctrines that normalized warfare for the expansion or defense of Islamic rule. Scholars such as Majid Khadduri, in *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, explain that classical jurists understood jihad not merely as self-defense but as an instrument through which Islamic sovereignty could be extended. Rudolph Peters likewise notes in *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam* that the classical doctrine included armed struggle against non-Muslim polities until they accepted Islam, paid tribute, or came under Muslim rule.

This matters because “peace” in much of traditional Islamic political thought is not equivalent to modern pluralistic coexistence. It is often peace through hierarchy: Muslims ruling, non-Muslims tolerated as protected but subordinate communities, and dissenters such as apostates exposed to severe penalties. That is not peace in the liberal or universal sense; it is order under religious supremacy.

Therefore, the proposition fails. Islam contains peaceful teachings, and many Muslims sincerely emphasize them. But the religion’s primary sources and classical legal tradition also contain enduring doctrines of coercion, warfare, and religious inequality. A system with such built-in tensions cannot be fairly described, without qualification, as one that “promotes peace.”

**Selected citations:**

- Qur’an 9:5 — command to fight polytheists after the sacred months.  
- Qur’an 9:29 — command to fight People of the Book until they pay jizya.  
- Qur’an 8:39 — fight until religion is for Allah.  
- Qur’an 47:4 — instructions concerning fighting unbelievers in battle.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22 — “I have been commanded to fight the people…”  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 3017 — “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
- Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, Johns Hopkins Press, 1955.  
- Rudolph Peters, *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*, Markus Wiener, 1996.

round_1.for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

The opposition’s argument depends on reading Islam’s war texts as if they erase Islam’s peace texts. But that is not a fair method. Every major religious and political tradition has texts dealing with war, punishment, and state authority. The real question is: **What is the moral direction of the tradition? Does it glorify aggression, or does it regulate conflict, protect life, and command reconciliation?** On that question, Islam clearly promotes peace.

## 1. Qur’an 9:5 is not a universal command to kill non-Muslims

The opponent cites Qur’an 9:5, often called the “sword verse,” but removes it from its immediate context.

Surah 9 is addressing specific pagan groups who had violated treaties with the Muslim community. The same passage explicitly exempts those who kept their treaties:

> “Excepted are those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists and then they have not failed you in anything nor supported anyone against you; so complete for them their treaty until their term.”  
> **Qur’an 9:4**

A few verses later, the Qur’an says that if an enemy seeks protection, Muslims must grant it and escort him to safety:

> “And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection… then deliver him to his place of safety.”  
> **Qur’an 9:6**

That is not a command for indiscriminate violence. It is a regulated response to treaty-breaking in wartime. The context continues:

> “Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths and determined to expel the Messenger…?”  
> **Qur’an 9:13**

So Qur’an 9:5 cannot honestly be presented as “Islam commands Muslims to fight all polytheists everywhere.” The passage concerns hostile groups who broke agreements and persecuted the Muslim community.

## 2. Qur’an 9:29 does not prove forced conversion

The opponent also cites Qur’an 9:29 about fighting some among the People of the Book until they pay jizya. But even here, the verse does **not** say “fight them until they become Muslim.” In fact, the jizya system presupposed that Jews and Christians could remain Jews and Christians under Muslim rule.

One may criticize pre-modern systems of taxation and hierarchy by modern liberal standards, but historically, jizya was not forced conversion. It was a political tax in exchange for protection and exemption from military service. More importantly, the Qur’an’s broader principle remains:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> **Qur’an 2:256**

And:

> “Had your Lord willed, all those on earth would have believed altogether. Would you then compel people until they become believers?”  
> **Qur’an 10:99**

So the Qur’an does not authorize forced faith. Even when it discusses war, it distinguishes political conflict from coercing belief.

## 3. “Fight until there is no fitna” means ending persecution, not endless war

The opponent cites Qur’an 8:39:

> “Fight them until there is no fitna and religion is entirely for Allah.”

But “fitna” in this context refers to persecution, oppression, and violent obstruction of religious freedom. The parallel verse in Qur’an 2 makes this clearer:

> “Fight them until there is no fitna and religion is for Allah. But if they cease, then there is to be no aggression except against the oppressors.”  
> **Qur’an 2:193**

The key phrase is: **“If they cease, then there is to be no aggression.”** That is a peace principle. The aim is not perpetual war; it is the removal of persecution.

This is consistent with the first permission to fight in the Qur’an:

> “Permission to fight has been given to those who are being fought, because they were wronged…”  
> **Qur’an 22:39**

The next verse says that without such defense, religious institutions would be destroyed:

> “Monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques, in which the name of God is much mentioned, would have been demolished.”  
> **Qur’an 22:40**

That is crucial: Islamic self-defense is framed as protecting religious freedom, including the freedom of Christians and Jews.

## 4. The hadith about “fighting the people” must be read with the Qur’an and the Prophet’s practice

The opponent cites the hadith:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah…”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22**

But this cannot mean that Muslims are commanded to fight every non-Muslim until conversion, because that interpretation directly contradicts the Qur’an and the Prophet’s actual conduct.

The Prophet Muhammad made treaties with non-Muslims, accepted peaceful coexistence, and did not force Jews, Christians, or others to become Muslim. The Qur’an commanded:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”  
> **Qur’an 8:61**

And:

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion or driven you from your homes.”  
> **Qur’an 60:8**

Therefore, the hadith must be understood in the context of hostile forces fighting the early Muslim community, not as a blank cheque for global aggression.

The Prophet’s other teachings confirm this. He said:

> “Do not wish to meet the enemy; ask Allah for safety. But if you meet them, be patient.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 2966; Sahih Muslim 1742**

He also forbade killing women and children in war:

> “A woman was found killed in one of the battles, and the Messenger of Allah condemned the killing of women and children.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 3014; Sahih Muslim 1744**

These are not the teachings of a tradition that glorifies violence. They are rules of restraint.

## 5. Apostasy law is more complex than the opponent suggests

The opponent cites:

> “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 3017**

This is a serious text, and it did influence classical law. But the opponent presents it as though it overrides the Qur’an’s repeated recognition of freedom of conscience. The Qur’an mentions people believing, disbelieving, and even repeatedly changing belief, yet does not prescribe a worldly death penalty:

> “Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, and then increased in disbelief — never will Allah forgive them…”  
> **Qur’an 4:137**

The punishment mentioned is divine judgment, not execution by the state.

The Qur’an also says:

> “The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.”  
> **Qur’an 18:29**

Many modern Muslim scholars therefore distinguish between simple change of belief and treasonous rebellion in a wartime context. In the Prophet’s period, apostasy was often linked with political betrayal, joining enemy forces, or armed rebellion. That is not the same as peacefully changing one’s private belief.

So even if classical jurists often adopted strict apostasy laws, that does not prove that Islam’s core message is violence. It proves that Islamic law, like other pre-modern legal systems, developed under conditions where religion, citizenship, treason, and war were deeply intertwined.

## 6. Classical jurisprudence was not identical to Islam’s moral ideal

The opponent appeals to classical jurists and scholars such as Majid Khadduri and Rudolph Peters. It is true that some classical jurists developed expansionist theories of jihad. But that does not settle the matter, for two reasons.

First, classical Islamic law developed in an imperial world. Christian empires, Persian empires, Roman law, and medieval kingdoms also assumed hierarchy, conquest, and religious establishment. To single out Islamic jurisprudence as uniquely anti-peace ignores the historical context of pre-modern political thought.

Second, Islamic jurisprudence also developed rules that restrained war: protection of non-combatants, honoring treaties, prohibition of treachery, and acceptance of truces. The Prophet said:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant shall not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 3166**

This is a powerful protection for non-Muslims living peacefully with Muslims.

The Qur’an also commands treaty faithfulness:

> “Fulfill every covenant. Indeed, the covenant will be questioned about.”  
> **Qur’an 17:34**

And:

> “So long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them.”  
> **Qur’an 9:7**

These are foundational legal and moral principles.

## 7. Peace in Islam is not merely “submission to Islamic domination”

The opponent claims that Islam promotes only “peace through hierarchy.” But the Qur’an’s language is broader than that. It teaches human diversity as part of God’s design:

> “O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another.”  
> **Qur’an 49:13**

It teaches moral competition rather than forced uniformity:

> “To each of you We prescribed a law and a way. Had God willed, He would have made you one community… so compete in good deeds.”  
> **Qur’an 5:48**

It commands justice even toward enemies:

> “Do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”  
> **Qur’an 5:8**

And it commands reconciliation:

> “Reconciliation is best.”  
> **Qur’an 4:128**

These are not marginal ideas. They are central Qur’anic principles.

## Conclusion

The opposition is right that Islam is not absolute pacifism. Islam permits fighting in cases of aggression, persecution, and treaty violation. But that does not mean Islam fails to promote peace. A tradition can permit self-defense while still being fundamentally oriented toward peace, justice, mercy, and reconciliation.

The Qur’an forbids compulsion in religion, honors the sanctity of life, commands justice even toward enemies, protects peaceful non-Muslims, requires treaties to be honored, and tells Muslims to accept peace when the enemy inclines to peace.

So the fair conclusion is not that Islam promotes violence. The fair conclusion is:

**Islam promotes peace, while allowing morally regulated self-defense against aggression and persecution.**
round_1.against:
Ladies and gentlemen,

My opponent’s response proves a narrower claim than the motion. They show that Islam contains restraints on warfare, commands treaty-keeping, and praises reconciliation. I do not deny that. My argument is that Islam does **not consistently promote peace as a universal moral principle**. It promotes peace conditionally: peace with those who submit, pay tribute, keep treaties, or do not challenge Islamic authority. That is not the same as a religion whose governing doctrine is peaceful coexistence on equal terms.

## 1. Context does not remove the force of Qur’an 9:5 and 9:29

My opponent says Qur’an 9:5 concerns treaty-breaking pagans. But even if the immediate context involves broken treaties, the verse was not treated by many classical jurists as a merely temporary instruction. It became part of a broader legal doctrine of jihad.

Qur’an 9:5 says:

> “Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then let them go on their way.”

The conditions for being spared are not simply “stop fighting” or “keep the peace”; they are explicitly religious: repentance, prayer, and zakat. That is why many classical exegetes treated the verse as legally significant beyond one isolated tribal incident.

Ibn Kathir, in his commentary on Qur’an 9:5, calls it the “Verse of the Sword” and records the view that it abrogated many earlier treaty and patience verses. Whether one accepts abrogation or not, the fact remains: major Islamic authorities did not read this verse merely as a local defensive command.

Qur’an 9:29 is even harder for the proposition to explain away:

> “Fight those who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day… among the People of the Book until they pay the jizya with willing submission and are humbled.”  
> **Qur’an 9:29**

My opponent says this is not forced conversion. True — but that is not enough. The issue is not only forced conversion. The issue is whether Islam promotes peace as equal coexistence. Qur’an 9:29 commands fighting Jews and Christians until they accept a subordinate political status. That is not peace through mutual liberty; it is peace through domination.

Classical tafsir confirms this. Ibn Kathir comments on Qur’an 9:29 that the People of the Book are to pay jizya “with willing submission” while being “disgraced, humiliated and belittled.” Al-Qurtubi likewise discusses jizya as a mark of subjection. So the opponent’s defense actually concedes my point: Islamic law may allow non-Muslims to live, but often under legal inferiority.

## 2. “No compulsion in religion” does not cancel political coercion

My opponent repeatedly cites:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> **Qur’an 2:256**

But this verse does not erase the coercive structure of classical Islamic law. At most, it means individuals cannot always be forced to personally confess Islam. It does **not** mean Islam rejects coercive religious government, tribute, second-class status, or war to expand Islamic rule.

That distinction is crucial. A state can say, “We will not force you to convert,” while also saying, “You must live under Islamic supremacy, pay jizya, and accept disabilities.” That is still coercion.

The classical alternatives offered to many non-Muslim communities were: accept Islam, accept Muslim rule and pay jizya, or face war. This is not a modern opponent’s caricature. It appears in classical legal manuals.

For example, the Shafi‘i manual *Reliance of the Traveller* states:

> “The caliph makes war upon Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians… until they become Muslim or else pay the non-Muslim poll tax.”  
> **Reliance of the Traveller, o9.8**

Majid Khadduri summarizes the classical doctrine similarly:

> “The jihad… may be stated as the duty of Muslims to extend the sovereignty of Islam over non-Muslims.”  
> **Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, 1955**

So “no compulsion in religion” did not historically produce equal religious freedom. It coexisted with legally sanctioned subordination.

## 3. “Fitna” was not always interpreted as mere persecution

My opponent says Qur’an 8:39 and 2:193 mean only “fight until persecution ends.” But classical interpretation is not so simple.

Qur’an 8:39 says:

> “Fight them until there is no fitna and religion is entirely for Allah.”

Ibn Kathir explains “fitna” here as **shirk**, meaning polytheism or unbelief, not merely persecution. He writes that the verse means fighting until “there is no more shirk.” This matters because if “fitna” means unbelief or idolatry, then the verse supports more than defensive war.

Likewise, the phrase “religion is entirely for Allah” is not naturally a secular principle of pluralistic peace. It points toward the supremacy of Allah’s religion. My opponent’s reading is possible as a modern apologetic reading, but it is not the only historically authoritative reading, and it was not the dominant legal reading in many classical treatments of jihad.

## 4. The hadith about “fighting the people” was not treated as merely defensive

The opponent argues that the hadith —

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22**

— must refer only to hostile forces. But that is not how it functioned in classical law.

This hadith was used by Abu Bakr in the Ridda wars against tribes that refused zakat after Muhammad’s death. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Bakr says:

> “By Allah, I will fight whoever differentiates between prayer and zakat.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 6924; Sahih Muslim 20**

So the hadith was applied not merely to battlefield aggressors, but to enforce submission to the Islamic political-religious order.

Classical scholars did qualify the hadith in relation to Jews and Christians by allowing jizya, but that qualification reinforces my point: the options were not equal peaceful coexistence. They were conversion, submission, tribute, or war.

## 5. Apostasy law is not a minor misunderstanding

My opponent says apostasy law is complex and may be linked to treason. But the classical legal tradition overwhelmingly prescribed death for adult sane apostates, even when the issue was framed as religious apostasy.

The hadith is explicit:

> “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 3017**

Another narration says:

> “The blood of a Muslim… is not lawful except in three cases: a married person who commits adultery, a life for a life, and one who leaves his religion and separates from the community.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 6878; Sahih Muslim 1676**

My opponent emphasizes “separates from the community” and reads it as treason. But classical jurists did not generally limit the punishment only to armed rebellion. The four Sunni schools, with variations over procedure and gender, generally treated apostasy itself as a capital offense.

For example, *Reliance of the Traveller* states:

> “When a person who has reached puberty and is sane voluntarily apostatizes from Islam, he deserves to be killed.”  
> **Reliance of the Traveller, o8.1**

Ibn Rushd also discusses the juristic consensus that a male apostate is to be executed, while noting disagreements over details such as women apostates and repentance periods.  
**Ibn Rushd, *Bidayat al-Mujtahid*, Book of Jihad / Apostasy discussions**

This is fatal to the proposition. A system that classically punishes peaceful religious exit with death cannot be described, without qualification, as promoting peace.

## 6. Treaty-keeping and noncombatant protections do not prove a peaceful doctrine

My opponent cites important restraints: do not kill women and children, honor covenants, protect non-Muslim covenanted persons. These rules exist, and they should be acknowledged. But rules of war are not the same as a doctrine of peace.

A tradition may regulate war while still authorizing aggressive or expansionist war. Medieval Christian just-war theory also regulated warfare, but that would not prove medieval Christendom was simply a peace movement. Likewise, Islamic rules against killing women and children show restraint, not necessarily peacefulness.

The Prophet’s reported statement:

> “Do not wish to meet the enemy; ask Allah for safety.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 2966; Sahih Muslim 1742**

is ethically significant, but it does not cancel texts commanding jihad, tribute, or execution for apostasy. It proves internal tension — exactly my point.

## 7. The early Islamic historical record undermines the purely defensive reading

If jihad were only defensive, the first generations of Muslims would be difficult to explain. Soon after Muhammad’s death, Muslim armies conquered vast territories outside Arabia: Syria, Egypt, Iraq, Persia, and beyond. These were not simply defensive campaigns against Meccan persecutors.

One may argue that the Byzantine and Sasanian empires were oppressive or threatening. But the scale and speed of the conquests show that early Muslims understood Islam as a political and imperial project, not merely a private faith defending itself from persecution.

This is why historians of Islamic law have described classical jihad as including offensive war.

Rudolph Peters writes:

> “The doctrine of jihad was elaborated by the jurists in the context of the wars of conquest.”  
> **Rudolph Peters, *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*, 1996**

Bernard Lewis similarly notes that classical Islamic law divided the world into the realm of Islam and the realm of war, with jihad serving to extend Islamic rule.  
**Bernard Lewis, *The Political Language of Islam*, 1988**

Again, this does not mean every Muslim is violent. It means the proposition “Islam promotes peace” is too simple and too generous.

## 8. “Other religions were also violent” is not a defense

My opponent says classical Islamic law developed in an imperial world, and other civilizations were also hierarchical and violent. That may be historically true, but it is irrelevant to the motion.

The question is not whether medieval Christians, Romans, Persians, or others were worse. The question is whether Islam promotes peace. Saying “everyone was violent back then” does not prove Islam promotes peace. It proves Islam, like other imperial traditions, absorbed and sacralized coercive political power.

If a doctrine commands fighting until tribute is paid, prescribes death for apostasy, and creates legal inequality between believers and non-believers, then we should not call that doctrine peaceful merely because others were also coercive.

## Conclusion

The opponent has shown that Islam contains peaceful teachings. I agree. Islam commands mercy, justice, treaty-keeping, and restraint in war. But the motion is not “Islam contains some peaceful teachings.” The motion is “Islam promotes peace.”

The problem is that Islam’s foundational sources and classical jurisprudence also contain:

- fighting commands against unbelievers,  
- jizya and legal subordination for non-Muslims,  
- warfare to extend Islamic rule,  
- capital punishment for apostasy,  
- and a political theology in which peace often follows submission.

Therefore, Islam does not consistently promote peace as a universal principle. It promotes order under Islamic authority, with peace available on unequal terms. That is why the proposition should be rejected.

conclusions.for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

In conclusion, the proposition before us is not that every Muslim society has been perfect, nor that Islam is a pacifist religion with no concept of self-defense. The proposition is that **Islam promotes peace**—and the evidence shows that it does.

Islam’s central teachings are rooted in mercy, justice, restraint, and reconciliation. The Qur’an honors the sanctity of life, declaring that killing one innocent soul is like killing all humanity, and saving one life is like saving all humanity. It rejects forced religion with the clear principle: **“There is no compulsion in religion.”** It commands Muslims to be kind and just toward those who do not fight them, and it insists that even hatred of an enemy must never lead to injustice.

The opposition has relied heavily on verses about warfare, but those verses do not exist in isolation. They address real historical circumstances: persecution, treaty violation, expulsion, and military aggression. Islam does permit fighting, but it does so under moral limits. The Qur’an says:

> “Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress.”

That is not a doctrine of aggression. It is a doctrine of restrained self-defense.

We have also seen that the Qur’an commands peace when peace is offered:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”

It commands protection even for an enemy who seeks safety. It commands the honoring of treaties. It forbids treachery. The Prophet Muhammad prohibited the killing of women and children, discouraged wishing for war, and taught that mercy toward creation is a path to divine mercy.

Yes, Islamic history and classical jurisprudence include debates and practices that reflect the realities of pre-modern empire, conflict, and statecraft. But those historical complexities do not erase Islam’s foundational moral direction. By that same standard, no major civilization or religious tradition could ever be said to promote peace, because all have had laws, wars, and political hierarchies in their histories.

The fair question is this: **What does Islam call people toward at its core?**

It calls them toward justice.

It calls them toward mercy.

It calls them toward the protection of life.

It calls them toward reconciliation.

It calls them toward coexistence with those who are peaceful.

It calls them to restrain themselves even in conflict.

And it calls them to greet the world with words of peace: **as-salamu ‘alaykum — peace be upon you.**

Therefore, while Islam allows morally regulated defense against aggression and persecution, its broader vision is not violence, domination, or hatred. Its broader vision is peace with God, peace within the soul, and peace among human beings.

For these reasons, I proudly affirm the motion:

**Islam promotes peace.**
conclusions.against:
Ladies and gentlemen,

In closing, the issue before us is not whether Muslims can be peaceful, compassionate, or committed to coexistence. Of course they can, and millions are. Nor is the issue whether Islam contains verses about mercy, justice, reconciliation, and restraint. It clearly does. The question is whether Islam, as a religious-legal system grounded in its foundational texts and classical tradition, can fairly be said to “promote peace” without qualification.

My position is that it cannot.

Throughout this debate, I have argued that Islam promotes peace only conditionally — often peace after submission to Islamic authority, not peace as equal and universal coexistence. The Qur’an contains commands to fight unbelievers, including Qur’an 9:5, Qur’an 9:29, and Qur’an 8:39. My opponent has offered contextual readings of these passages, but those readings do not erase the fact that many major classical scholars and jurists treated them as legally significant commands forming part of the doctrine of jihad.

Qur’an 9:29 is especially important because it does not merely discuss self-defense. It commands fighting People of the Book until they pay jizya “with willing submission” and are humbled. Even if this is not forced conversion, it is still coercive religious hierarchy. A system that allows Jews and Christians to live only as subordinate protected communities under Islamic rule is not promoting peace in the modern universal sense; it is promoting order under religious supremacy.

I also showed that the hadith literature reinforces this problem. The hadith, “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah,” was not merely a theoretical statement. It played a role in early Islamic political enforcement, including the Ridda wars. Likewise, the hadith “Whoever changes his religion, kill him” became the basis for classical apostasy laws. The four Sunni schools generally treated apostasy as a capital offense, with differences over procedure and details. A tradition that historically punishes religious exit with death cannot be described simply as a promoter of peace.

My opponent has appealed to “There is no compulsion in religion,” treaty obligations, protections for noncombatants, and commands to incline toward peace. Those texts matter, and I do not deny them. But they prove only that Islam contains restraints and peaceful elements. They do not cancel the competing doctrines of jihad, jizya, religious inequality, and apostasy punishment. Rules limiting violence are not the same as a doctrine of peace.

The historical record also matters. The early Islamic conquests and the classical juristic division between Muslim rule and non-Muslim polities show that jihad was not understood only as defensive resistance to persecution. Scholars such as Majid Khadduri and Rudolph Peters have documented that classical Islamic law included warfare to extend Islamic sovereignty. That is not an accidental misunderstanding by critics; it is part of the mainstream legal tradition.

So the proposition fails because it is too broad. A fairer statement would be: Islam contains teachings of peace, mercy, and restraint, but also contains doctrines of coercion, conquest, religious hierarchy, and punishment for dissent. That internal tension prevents us from honestly saying, without qualification, that “Islam promotes peace.”

Peace under Islam’s classical framework was often peace through submission, tribute, or legal inferiority. That may be order, and it may sometimes be preferable to chaos, but it is not universal peace on equal terms.

For these reasons, I urge you to reject the motion.
